activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: In tropical rainforests, the difference between day and night temperatures can be larger than the difference between the warmest and coolest months.
story:
Grandpa's dining room table had become a science lab, and Austin was the scientist who had no idea what he was doing. Spread in front of him were two printed graphs for Ms. Gill's assignment: one showing monthly rainfall and temperature for the Sonoran Desert, the other for a rainforest in Brazil. His job was to compare the two climates, and his pencil hovered over the paper without writing anything.

"I need this to be interesting," Austin muttered, "because right now it's just squiggles."

His cousin Adele slid into the chair across from him, balancing a bowl of popcorn. Adele wanted one thing from the afternoon: to be entertained. "Then make it interesting," she said. "What do the squiggles say?"

"The desert gets almost no rain, and the rainforest gets tons of it. That part's easy." Austin tapped the temperature lines. "But here's the weird part. The desert graph swings from blazing hot months to freezing cold months. The rainforest graph barely moves. Warmest month, coolest month, it's all about the same."

"Sounds boring," Adele said, tossing a kernel at him. "Same temperature forever."

"It's not boring, it's..." Austin stopped. He leaned closer to the rainforest graph. Grandpa, drying dishes at the sink behind them, glanced over but said nothing. Austin flipped through his library book on rainforests and found a chart of hourly temperatures at a weather station. His eyes went down the column, and then he sat back like he'd been poked.

"Adele. Look at this. The days get hot and the nights get cool, right there in the numbers." He grabbed his pencil and circled the day's high and the night's low. Then he circled the warmest month and the coolest month on the other graph and compared the gaps. "The swing between day and night is bigger than the swing between the warmest and coolest months. Way bigger."

"So?" Adele said, stealing her own popcorn back.

"So if somebody was packing for the rainforest, they'd think, it's hot every month, I only need shorts. But the nights are cool. They'd need a sweater. In a rainforest." He laughed. "Ms. Gill is going to think I made this up."

"It does sound made up," Adele admitted. "Show me again."

Austin walked her through it line by line, testing his idea against both graphs to be sure he wasn't fooling himself. It seemed logical, but he'd been wrong before, like the time he'd sworn hail was frozen rain and Ms. Gill had gently proved otherwise in front of the whole class. He checked the book a second time, then a third. The numbers held.

"Fine," Adele said, pointing at his blank worksheet, where despair had been about to set in five minutes ago. "Write it down before you forget it. And draw a little person in a sweater."

"That's not scientific."

"I'll mediate," Grandpa said from the sink, without turning around. "One small sweater person, in the name of science."

Austin grinned and picked up his pencil.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: In hot deserts, the sun and dry air could evaporate far more water in a year than falls as rain, so the ground stays dry.
story:
Declan had planned to finish his climate project at home, in a house with air conditioning and a printer. Instead his grandfather had collected him from the airport and driven him to a place where the mailbox leaned like it was tired, and now the project had to happen here, in a kitchen in the Arizona desert, over a laptop that connected to the internet when it felt like it.

The assignment asked him to compare a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs. His friend Emy-Rose had the easy half. Her grandmother lived in Hilo, Hawaii, and Emy-Rose had already texted him a photo of her rain gauge with water in it, plus the smug caption "day one." Declan's grandfather owned no rain gauge. What he owned was a cactus, a watering can, and a patio that looked like the surface of a planet that had given up.

Declan started with the graphs. He printed them at the library in town: monthly rainfall bars for a hot desert and for a rainforest, and two temperature lines that both ran high. He laid them side by side on the kitchen table and tried to evaluate what he was seeing. The rainforest bars towered over the desert bars, which was almost embarrassing, since some of the desert bars were so short he had to squint to confirm they existed. He found the median monthly rainfall for each place, and the rainforest number was so much larger that he checked it twice, in case the library printer had made a typo.

The temperature lines were the part that bugged him. Both places were hot. If heat meant dryness, the rainforest should have been dry too, and it plainly was not, judging by Emy-Rose's photo of a puddle in her grandmother's driveway that had lasted three days. He needed a way to test the difference, and the laptop kept buffering, so the internet was not going to be influential in his thinking today. He went outside with a measuring cup and poured exactly one cup of water onto the flat concrete beside the patio, marking the puddle's edge with two pebbles.

Then he did what any scientist stuck in a desert does. He sat in a lawn chair and watched water do nothing. By ten o'clock the puddle had shrunk to a dark ring. By eleven the ring was gone, and the concrete was the same pale gray as everywhere else, and the sun was still climbing. He poured a second cup in the shade of the barbecue, out of some sense of fairness. That puddle lasted longer, but even it surrendered before lunch.

He called Emy-Rose that afternoon. "Question," he said. "The sun and dry air at my grandpa's could evaporate way more water in a year than falls as rain here. Like, a puddle I made this morning was gone before lunch. Is your puddle still there?"

"It's been there since Tuesday," Emy-Rose said. "Grandma says it's practically a pond now."

"So that's the whole difference," Declan said. "It's not just how much rain falls. It's how much the sky takes back." He wrote it at the top of his poster in marker, then drew the desert puddle as a ghost with an exit arrow.

That evening his grandfather came out with two glasses of lemonade, looked at the poster, and looked at the dry patio.

"Learn something today?" his grandfather asked.

"Learned you can't keep a puddle in this yard," Declan said, and taped the last graph down before the wind could evaluate it for him.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The marking 'a tempo' tells players to return to the original speed after the music has slowed down or sped up.
story:
Alice sat down at Ryerson's piano with the sheet music for "Moonlight Jig" in front of her. She had been practicing the piece for two weeks, and today was the last rehearsal before the school talent show. A stuffed koala grinned at her from the top of the piano, and she gave its grey marsupial face a pat for luck. "Ready?" she asked. Ryerson nodded and lifted the lid of the percussion box he kept beside the bench.

The first half went well. Alice's fingers found the bouncy opening, and Ryerson tapped the tambourine right on the beat, his wrist flicking in time with hers. Then they reached the middle, where the marking "rit." appeared above the staff. Alice slowed down, letting each note stretch out like taffy, and Ryerson followed her. It sounded beautiful, she thought, dreamy and strange. But when the next section began, something felt wrong. Ryerson's tambourine had gone quiet, and when she glanced over, his hand was hovering in midair, waiting.

"You're still slow," he said. "The whole last page is dragging." Alice frowned at the music. She played the passage again and listened hard. He was right. The slow feeling from the rit. had followed her all the way to the end, like mud stuck to her shoes. She bent closer to the page, wondering if there was a clue she had missed. There, printed small above the bar where the dreamy part ended, were two words: "a tempo." She traced them with her finger. "Rit." had told her to slow down. Did "a tempo" tell her something about speed too?

She tested a simple idea. "Play the opening speed," she said to Ryerson, "just the counting, nothing else." He clapped the original beat, quick and bright, and she matched her hands to his claps. Then she played from the "a tempo" marking forward while he kept time, and the melody sprang back to life, bouncing the way it had at the start. "That's it," she said. "A tempo means go back to the original speed after you've slowed down." Ryerson grinned and shook the koala at her like a maraca.

They ran the whole piece once more, and this time when the rit. came, Alice let the notes wander slow and soft, then snapped the speed back exactly where the marking told her to. The change matched the feel of the music, the way a heartbeat corresponds to what a body is doing, fast when it runs and calm when it rests. Ryerson's tambourine came in clean and sure, and by the final chord they were both laughing. Ms. Ramírez, who had come to pick up her nephew next door, stopped on the porch and applauded through the window. "Again," Ryerson said, tapping the tambourine against his palm. "From the top."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, which slowed the motion enough for him to time it.
story:
Julia crouched at the end of the hallway with a stopwatch in one hand and a marble in the other. Behind her, her dad held one end of a wooden board propped on a stack of dictionaries, making a steep little hill. The plan was simple: roll the marble down, time it, measure how far it went, and turn the numbers into a distance-time graph for Monday's lab report. Her teacher, Ms. Owusu, had been strict about enforcing the rule that every graph needed real measurements, not guesses, and Julia intended to follow it.

"Ready," she called. Her dad let go, the marble flashed down the board and shot across the floor, and Julia stabbed the button far too late. "Zero point two seconds? That can't be right." They tried again, and again, and every time the marble reached the wall before her thumb could catch up. On the fourth attempt she didn't even press the button. She sat back on her heels and groaned.

Amina's face appeared on the tablet screen, propped against the baseboard. She was supposed to be doing the same experiment in her own kitchen, and she wanted their graphs to match so their group could have the best data in the class. "Same problem here," Amina said. "My ball is faster than my thumb. Maybe we should just make up numbers that look nice."

"We can't," Julia said. "Ms. Owusu wants an objective measurement, something that doesn't depend on us deciding what it should be." She picked up the marble and turned it over in her fingers, thinking. Fast was the enemy. If the ball moved slower, she could actually time it. But how did you slow down a rolling ball without touching it? She looked at the board. The steeper the hill, the faster the marble flew. So a gentler slope might mean a gentler speed. "Dad, take away half the dictionaries."

He raised an eyebrow but lifted the stack down until the board lay at a low slant, more of a whisper than a hill. Julia marked the floor with masking tape every thirty centimeters, the way Ms. Owusu had shown them, and set the marble at the top. When her dad released it, the marble crept down the ramp and rolled along the tiles at a pace she could actually watch. She clicked the stopwatch at each strip of tape, calling out, "One! Two! Three!" while Amina scribbled the times on her own sheet of paper, miles away but shouting them back anyway.

They ran it three times to be sure, and the numbers came out almost the same every trial. Julia plotted them on graph paper, distance going up one side, time going along the bottom, and the dots fell into a nearly straight line climbing from the corner. She stared at it. She had expected a wobbly scatter, but the points behaved like they were following a rule she couldn't see, some hidden law of rolling things that only showed up on paper.

Then her dad leaned over her shoulder. "You know, you're not the first person to try this trick. Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, because the ramps slowed the motion enough for him to time it." Julia sat back, amazed that a scientist from centuries ago had faced the exact same problem in the exact same way, without stopwatches or masking tape or a video call.

"Then we did it right," Amina said through the speaker. "Send me a picture of that graph before my dad confiscates my tablet for the night. He claims my science homework is bad for his beauty sleep, which is basically a crime against commerce, since I'm his daughter and he should be investing in me."

Julia laughed and photographed the graph, the line of dots marching upward like a staircase. "Best data in the class," she said, and taped the graph to the refrigerator door, right at eye level, where nobody walking past could miss it.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Xylitol, a sweetener in some sugar-free gum and candy, makes a dog's body release insulin and can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar.
story:
Cooper leaned over the counter at the pet store while the cashier lifted a wriggling beagle puppy into his arms. "His name's yours to pick," she said. Cooper had already decided on Biscuit, because the puppy was the exact color of one. Moses and Philemon crowded in beside him, arguing about whether Biscuit would sleep in a crate or a dog bed, and Mr. Traoré, who had driven them all here, checked his watch for the third time.

At home, Cooper set up the water bowl, the food dish, and the puppy's bed in the corner of his room. Biscuit explored everything, sneezed at the cedar shavings, and then disappeared under the desk. Cooper got down on his knees to look. Curious thing: the puppy wasn't just wandering. He kept returning to sniff one spot, Cooper's backpack, which lay on the floor with its flap partway open.

"Hey," Cooper said to himself. What was in there that smelled so interesting? He emptied the backpack onto his bed. Pencils, a crumpled worksheet, three gum wrappers, and a strip of sugar-free gum, still in its foil, half pushed out of the pack. Cooper picked it up and turned it toward the window, squinting at the tiny ingredients like he was looking through a magnifying lens. He saw the word xylitol, printed small. He'd read the label at the store out of boredom while his mom paid, and something about it had stuck: xylitol, a sweetener in some sugar-free gum and candy, makes a dog's body release insulin and can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar.

He wondered whether one strip could really matter. He couldn't see inside Biscuit's body, couldn't watch insulin or blood sugar doing anything, so how would he even know? Maybe the puppy seemed fine now, but maybe the trouble came later. Cooper decided not to guess. First he would verify that Biscuit hadn't already eaten any. He checked the wrappers: all three were old ones from his own pocket, dry and flattened, no tooth marks. The foil strip was whole and sealed. Then, to be sure, he counted the pieces left in the pack and counted them again an hour later. Same number.

"I'm not taking chances anyway," he told Moses on the phone that night. "Xylitol," Moses repeated, like the word tasted strange. "That stuff is in candy too, not just gum. My aunt says her dog isn't immune to any of it, even the tiny amounts." Cooper carried the gum downstairs and handed it to his dad, who dropped it in the outside trash can and clamped the lid down.

Biscuit slept in a heap on the new bed after all, one ear flopped over his nose. Cooper knelt beside him and watched the puppy's ribs rise and fall, slow and steady, and he made a mental list of everything else he'd check tomorrow: the candy dish on the coffee table, the granola bars in his lunchbox, the pockets of his jacket. Biscuit's tail thumped once against the cushion, even in his sleep.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: With regular use, the brain adapts to nicotine, so a person needs more of it to feel the same effect; this is called tolerance.
story:
The health elective at Camp Windrow ended with each camper teaching a five-minute lesson on the stage, and Ava had drawn the hardest topic in the jar: how nicotine hooks the brain. She understood the reward pathway well enough to draw it, dopamine sliding into receptors like a key into a lock. What she could not figure out was why her uncle kept saying his vaping habit used to be one pod a week and was now three. If nicotine worked the same way every time, the amount should stay the same.

She spread her poster on the picnic table while Cedar painted arrows and Nahla arranged red buttons for the dopamine. "The brain adapts," Nahla read off Ava's messy notes from the pharmacy trip last weekend, when they had walked to town for sunscreen. "That's what the pharmacist told you?" Ava nodded. She had asked about her uncle, and the pharmacist had said that with regular use, the brain adapts to nicotine, so a person needs more of it to feel the same effect. Then Ava had asked what that was called, and the pharmacist had smiled and said one word: "Tolerance." That word had been sitting in her pocket all week like a stone.

"But how do I show it?" Ava said, tapping the poster. "Nobody can see a brain adapting." Cedar suggested drawing a brain wearing tiny sunglasses. Nahla suggested a rap. Ava stared at the red buttons instead, and an idea arrived, not slowly but all at once, the way spontaneous ideas do. She scooped the buttons into a cup. "Okay, you're the brain," she told Cedar. "Every time I dump five buttons, that's a puff. You inhale, dopamine floods in, you feel great. Show me great." Cedar spread his arms wide and grinned like a cartoon.

Ava dumped five buttons, and Cedar grinned. She dumped five again, and he grinned smaller. On the fifth dump, Cedar barely smiled. "What if," Ava said slowly, "the brain gets used to it, so the same amount stops working?" She tried dumping eight buttons, and Cedar's grin came back full force. Then ten, then twelve, his grin snapping to full brightness only as the numbers climbed. Nahla scribbled the counts on the poster's edge. By the end of the row, the cup was almost empty and Cedar was grinning at fourteen.

"You realize," Cedar said, still grinning, "you just used up all my buttons being addicted." "That's the whole point," Ava said. "It never gets easier, only bigger." Nahla looked at the scribbled numbers, twelve, fourteen, climbing in a ragged line, and said quietly that her cousin had said almost exactly that in April, laughing like it was nothing.

On the last morning, Ava stood on the stage with her cup and her poster. She pointed at the climbing numbers, said the word tolerance out loud once, and then dumped buttons over Cedar's head while he grinned bigger and bigger and bigger, until the cup was empty and his hands were held out for more.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift after spellings had started to become fixed, which is a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation.
story:
The school bus rattled over the pothole by the gym, and Mackenzie's word list jumped in her hands. She was down to the last page before the county spelling bee, and the words were betraying her. "Bite," she muttered. "B-I-T-E. Why is that e even there? It doesn't make a sound. It's just sitting there like camouflage, pretending to be useful."

Ali leaned over from the seat across the aisle. "You're the one who signed up for this."

"And I can spell everything except the words with sneaky letters." She tapped the paper. "Bite, bone, home. Then bite's weird cousin, bit. One letter changes the whole sound and I can't see why."

Henley, two rows back, poked her head over the seat. "Maybe the letters used to make those sounds and then stopped. Like, the e used to say something."

Mackenzie stared at her. That was actually a thought. If the e had once been pronounced, the spellings wouldn't be strange at all. They'd be records of something that changed. She flipped her list over and wrote out loud sounds with her pencil, mouthing "bee-nay" for bone just to test it, and Ali burst out laughing so hard the eighth graders turned around.

Mr. Adebayo, riding up front with the team, held up a battered paperback. "You'll want this," he said, and passed it back along the seats. Mackenzie found the page he'd marked. Her eyes went wide. "Listen to this. Between about 1400 and 1700, the long vowel sounds all shifted. It's called the Great Vowel Shift." She read faster. "And here's the twist. Printing had already locked the spellings in, so the letters stayed put while the sounds walked off without them."

"So the e isn't camouflage," Henley said. "It's a fossil."

"A fossil that bites," Ali said, and Mackenzie's grin was infectious; even the eighth graders were smiling now.

The bee that afternoon went three rounds before the announcer said "knife." Mackenzie pictured the word's history like a map, the k that had once been spoken, the strange old spellings that no longer matched the sounds. "K-N-I-F-E," she said. The judge nodded, and in the fourth round, when the word was "mimic," she was so relaxed she almost laughed. "M-I-M-I-C. Mimic."

Afterward Ali pretended to be the announcer, mimicking his deep voice. "Our next word is" and she held up a silent, invisible letter e, floating in the air like a tiny trophy.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Research on children at overnight camps has found that most campers feel at least some homesickness during their stay, and for most of them it stays mild.
story:
Avery had counted the hours until lights-out, and now that it was here, she wished she hadn't. The bunk above her creaked whenever Hugo moved, which was often. Somewhere across the cabin, Cassius was pretending to be asleep, but his breathing was too even, too perfect, like a kid performing sleep for an audience. Avery stared at the underside of Hugo's mattress and thought about her kitchen, where the light above the stove was probably on right now. Was she the only one doing this? It felt like a thing no one would admit out loud, which meant there was no way to know for sure. Unless there was.

The next morning she borrowed a marker from the craft bin and taped a scrap of paper to the inside of the bathroom door, where every girl in the cabin would see it and no counselor would. It said: if you miss home, draw one tally mark. She told herself she was being objective about it, like a scientist counting results instead of guessing. By dinner there were eleven tallies. Eleven, out of twelve girls.

That should have made her feel better, but it didn't, quite. She was the one who had put up the paper, so she knew about all eleven. Everyone else still thought they were alone. That was the problem with hidden things. A feeling nobody shows can't be discovered by accident; something has to happen out in the open.

She found her chance at the campfire. Mr. Desir had just finished a story about an enormous fish and gone off to talk to the lifeguard, and the coals were settling into that stage where you could actually hear yourself think. Hugo was hunched over his marshmallow stick, uncharacteristically quiet, and Avery wondered if he was homesick and if his joking usually hid it. She decided to test the idea out loud.

"I miss my dog," she said, to nobody in particular. "Like, a lot. I keep thinking he's waiting by the door."

Hugo looked up so fast his marshmallow slid into the fire. "You do? I miss my mom's cooking so bad I dreamed about scrambled eggs." Cassius leaned over from the next log. "I wrote my little brother a letter and I'm not even sure he can read."

Then came the twist. Mr. Desir, settling back onto his log, said, "Every summer, kids think they're the only one. But research on overnight camps found most campers feel at least some homesickness, and for most of them it stays mild." He said it like he was remarking on the weather, then asked who wanted seconds on marshmallows, and half the circle raised their hands.

"Wait," Hugo said. "Most? Like, most of everybody?"

"Most," said Cassius slowly, like he was working a math problem. "So it's basically normal. We've all just been hiding it in a way that, like, hindered us from finding each other."

"That's the weirdest use of hinder I've ever heard," Avery said, and the whole log of boys cracked up.

Later, at lights-out, Avery pulled her flashlight out from under her pillow. She didn't need it to find the bathroom paper; she knew the number by heart. But she clicked it on anyway and swept it once around the cabin, a slow circle over eleven sleeping shapes. In the beam each face looked the same: ordinary, breathing, here. Somewhere in her head a thought drifted past, that in a hundred years everyone in this cabin would be gone, a kind of extinction that even tallies and flashlights couldn't reach, and that this was somehow exactly why the tallies mattered now. She clicked the light off.

"Avery?" Hugo's voice came down through the mattress springs. "You still awake?"

"Yeah."

"Tomorrow can we put the tally paper somewhere the boys can use it too?"

Avery smiled into the dark. "Bring a marker," she said.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The crowd 'wave' became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, so many English speakers outside North America call it the Mexican wave.
story:
Aria had saved her allowance for two months to buy four tickets in the upper deck, and now she sat between her dad and her cousin Sofia, who had arrived from England three days earlier. Kaelyn and Myla were one row down, sharing a bag of popcorn and arguing about which team would score first. Below them the field gleamed under the lights, and the players were still warming up.

When Sofia found their seats, Aria had promised her a proper stadium experience, and part of that, in Aria's opinion, was the wave. Around the sixth inning, a section near third base started it. Thousands of people stood, threw their arms up, and sat down again, and the standing moved around the bowl like water sloshing in a giant cup. Aria jumped up with the rest of her section, yelling, then plopped back down, grinning.

"What is this called?" Sofia asked, pointing as the wave came around again.

"The wave," Aria said. "You know, the wave."

"We call it the Mexican wave," Sofia said.

Aria frowned. That didn't make sense. There was nothing Mexican about a baseball stadium in their own city. Maybe Sofia had made a mistake, or maybe she was teasing, the way she had teased Aria about the word "biscuit" at dinner. But Sofia was already standing with the next pass of the wave, so Aria filed the question away and jumped up with her.

She tested the idea the way she tested things, by asking around. "Excuse me," she said to the man with the foam finger at the end of the row. "Do you know why some people call the wave the Mexican wave?" The man shrugged. Myla said she'd heard her grandmother in Colombia say it that way too, though Myla wasn't sure why. Kaelyn was pessimistic about the whole project. "Nobody knows," she said. "You'll just embarrass yourself asking strangers." Aria kept asking anyway.

In the eighth inning, a fan a few seats over, an older woman wearing a scarf from a club team, overheard the girls talking and leaned in. "It got famous at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico," she said. "That's why, in a lot of English-speaking places outside North America, it's the Mexican wave." Aria turned to Sofia. "So it's the same thing, just a different name." Sofia nodded, looking a little smug, in Aria's opinion.

On the walk to the exit after the final out, Aria made a quiet amendment to her mental list of things Sofia knew more about than she did: biscuits, football versus soccer, and now this. Myla was still grumbling that her question had been better. "You didn't even have a question," Kaelyn said. "Yes I did," Myla said. "I asked why the hot dogs cost eight dollars." Sofia laughed so hard she had to stop walking. "Now that," she said, "nobody in the world can explain."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means a faster speed.
story:
Antoine crouched at the end of the gym hallway with a tennis ball, a meter stick, and a stopwatch he had borrowed from Ms. Mercer, who had one rule that afternoon: no running in the hallways, which prohibited anything but rolling. His problem was simple and stubborn. He wanted to know how fast his ball actually went, and eyeballing it told him nothing. Speed was invisible. You could not watch it, only chase it with numbers.

He had written a note to himself that morning, folded into his pocket like a tiny letter to his future self, and now he smoothed it out on the floor. Measure distance. Measure time. Divide. Annie, who was working beside him with a golf ball, leaned over to read it. "You wrote yourself instructions?" she said. "Last month I did the lab without a plan and got everything backwards," Antoine said. "This time I have a technique. Mark every meter, start the watch at zero distance, record where the ball is at each second." Annie tapped the paper. "Then we'll see if my ball beats yours."

Beatrix stood at the two-meter mark with her own stopwatch, calling out the seconds. At one second, Antoine's tennis ball had gone one meter. At two seconds, two meters. At three, three. Annie's golf ball was slower: one meter at one second, one and a half at two, two at three. Antoine wrote each number down, then drew two axes on graph paper and plotted the points, one line for each ball.

That was where the argument started, because the two lines crossed on his page and Annie insisted the crossing meant her ball had won. Antoine studied the graph. His line climbed like a ramp; hers rose gently, more flat than steep. "Look at yours," he said, tracing it with his finger. "A steeper line means a faster speed. Mine is steeper the whole way. Your ball is slower." Annie frowned at the page, then at the hallway, checking the paper against the world. "Then why did the lines cross?" she asked. Beatrix pointed at the vertical axis. "Because we started the golf ball half a meter ahead, that's all. The lines crossing isn't about speed. The steepness is."

Annie was quiet for a moment, rolling the golf ball back and forth under her palm. "So we didn't tie," she said. Antoine didn't answer right away. He remembered last month's backwards lab, how he had guessed instead of measuring, and how much easier guessing had been. He almost told her the graph might be wrong too. Instead he handed her the stopwatch. "Run it again," he said. "Authentic data, three trials. If your line gets steeper than mine, you win."

Annie set the golf ball on the floor, lined it up with the meter mark, and pressed the button. The ball whispered down the tiles, and Beatrix's voice rang out, "One second!"

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A guinea pig's front teeth never stop growing, so it needs things to chew on to wear them down.
story:
Victor held the cardboard carrier with both hands while Ms. Szabó from the animal shelter slid the paperwork across the counter. "His name is Biscuit," she said, "and he's been waiting three months for a home." Inside, a brown-and-white guinea pig with a white patch over one eye sniffed the air hole and made a sound like a tiny squeaky door. Victor's arms tingled from the weight, which was strange because Biscuit couldn't have weighed more than a bag of sugar.

On Monday, Victor set up the cage in his room: wood shavings, a little wooden house, a water bottle, and a food dish. His friend Mckinley came over after school and pressed her face to the bars. "He's so round," she said. "Like a furry potato." Mckinley wanted a pet of her own more than anything, but her building didn't allow animals, so she had promised herself she would learn everything about guinea pigs anyway, becoming Victor's unofficial mentor on the subject. She had checked out four library books and read two of them already.

The trouble started on Wednesday. Victor heard a metallic rattling in the night, steady as a dripping tap. In the morning he found Biscuit gripping the cage bars with his teeth, gnawing, gnawing, gnawing. "Maybe he's hungry," Victor said, and filled the food dish. Biscuit ate, then went right back to the bars. Mckinley frowned. "He's not hungry. Something else is going on."

Victor decided to test it. He put a carrot stick through the bars, and Biscuit attacked it, gnawing the same way but on the carrot instead of metal. Then a twig from the apple tree in the yard, then a toilet paper tube. Biscuit chewed everything, and his mood turned calm, almost sleepy, afterward. "It's not the cage he wants," Victor said slowly. "It's the chewing itself." They looked it up in one of Mckinley's library books, and there it was: a guinea pig's front teeth never stop growing, so it needs things to chew on to wear them down.

"So the bar gnawing was like an alarm," Mckinley said. "He was telling us his teeth needed work." Victor felt a little embarrassed he hadn't figured it out sooner, but Mckinley just started a chart. At the top she wrote CHEW MENU, and together they listed what Biscuit liked best. The volatile moods Victor had noticed, the squeaky complaining in the evening, settled down once the chewing box appeared next to the cage, stocked with hay twists and cardboard.

On Saturday they brought Zain over to see the results. Zain leaned in, and Biscuit, instead of rattling the bars, calmly picked up a hay twist and dragged it into his little wooden house. Zain raised his eyebrows. "He's like a tiny lumberjack," he said. Mckinley pointed at the chart, and Victor realized he could paraphrase the whole system in one sentence: keep the chew box full, and Biscuit stays happy. He refilled the box that afternoon and set it by the cage door.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect.
story:
Hailey spread six paper airplanes across the workbench in her family's garage, fanning them like cards. The light from the single bulb caught the fold lines, and the smell of motor oil drifted over from her dad's half of the bench. Her project was due in nine days, and she still didn't have clean results.

She had tested every plane that afternoon, throwing each one three times from the chalk mark on the driveway and pacing off the distance. Plane A had gone eleven steps, then seven, then fourteen. Plane D had barely cleared the recycling bin. The numbers were a mess, and the mess was starting to irritate her. She jabbed her pencil at the notebook. "This is supposed to be about wing shape," she muttered. "Wing shape."

A text buzzed on the phone beside the tape. It was from her classmate Haley: "Bad news. Erik says your project is wrong on the board. He says distance is your independent variable, because it's the important one. He was really vigorous about it. Kind of loud. Also, did you know the word for when a species dies out forever is extinction? Random quiz fact from my brother. See you Monday."

Hailey stared at the message, then at her data table. She read her own question aloud, written in marker at the top of the display board: "How does wing shape affect how far a paper airplane flies?" Erik had it backward, she was almost sure. The independent variable is the one thing a scientist changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is what gets measured to see the effect. She changed the wing shape on purpose. She measured the distance.

But then she looked at the planes again, and the almost-sure feeling wobbled. Plane A had narrow wings and thin paper. Plane B had wide wings and thick paper. Plane C had swept wings, thick paper, and a paperclip on the nose. Her hands had stopped halfway through folding, and she set the planes down slowly. She hadn't changed only one thing. She had changed wing shape and paper weight and nose weight all at once, which was exactly why the numbers jumped around. The distance wasn't responding to the wing shape alone; it was responding to everything mixed together.

She spent that evening and half of Saturday refolding. One stack of identical paper, one paperclip on every nose, six planes exactly alike except for the wings. Then she threw them again from the chalk mark, thirty throws in all, while the neighbor's cat watched from the fence with polite interest.

On Monday she found Erik by the lockers. "You said distance is my independent variable," she said. "It's the other way around. The independent variable is the one thing I change on purpose, the wing shape. Distance is the dependent variable. It's what I measure to see the effect."

Erik frowned at her new chart, all six columns lined up in a neat upward slope, wide wings to narrow. He read it twice. "Huh," he said. "That makes more sense than my way." He handed the chart back and tapped the farthest column. "So what flew longest?"

Hailey grinned. "You'll have to come to the fair and find out."

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In German, links means left, rechts means right, and geradeaus means straight ahead.
story:
Mya spread the map of her made-up town across the kitchen table and pulled a scarf out of the drawer. "Bennett, you're the tourist," she said. "Evelina, blindfold on."

Evelina tied the scarf over her eyes and held her arms out in front of her, waiting. It was Sunday afternoon, and on Tuesday their class had a German speaking test where they had to ask for directions and understand the answer. Bennett wanted the top mark in the class, and he had announced on the bus that he intended to get it, so he had come over with his flashcards and refused to leave until they drilled for an hour.

Bennett read from his card. "Entschuldigung, wo ist die Bank?"

"Go straight ahead, then, um." Mya checked her notes. "Links." She watched Evelina walk forward, then turn, and Evelina's shin cracked against the table leg. Evelina laughed, but Mya didn't. She had said the word for left, she was almost sure, except Evelina had turned right. Or maybe the notes were right and Evelina had turned the wrong way. She couldn't tell which of them had made the mistake, and that was the problem. On Tuesday she would get one chance to hear the answer, and there would be no way to check her notes.

She remembered Wednesday, when Ms. Oliveira had pulled the blinds down and called Bennett to the front of the room. He had been blindfolded too, and the class had whispered directions to him while he crept between the desks. Every time someone said links he had gone left, and every time someone said rechts he had gone right, and once someone said geradeaus and he had walked straight into the bookshelf, which had made everyone laugh, including Ms. Oliveira. Mya closed her eyes and replayed it. Links meant left. Rechts meant right. Geradeaus meant straight ahead. Her instinct had been to trust her messy notes over her own memory, but the memory was clearer than the page.

She had an idea, and she needed to test it. She slid the table out of Evelina's path, adjusted the scarf so it sat firmly over Evelina's eyes, and stood behind her. "Okay, new rule. No notes." Bennett straightened up, because this was exactly the kind of challenge he liked. "Ich suche die Post," he said.

"Geradeaus," said Mya, "dann rechts." Evelina walked to the end of the kitchen, turned right, and stopped exactly at the refrigerator, which was the post office on their map. Bennett let out a groan and shuffled his cards.

"Again," he said. "Faster this time."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can help a person focus, such as before a test or a race.
story:
The list of audition times hung outside the music room, and Kayla's name was third, right after Tayla's. She had signed up for the spring solo on a brave day in September, but now it was January, and her hands were cold and her stomach kept flipping. "You look like you're about to be sick," said Naomie, who was holding Kayla's sheet music because Kayla's fingers wouldn't stay still.

"I think it's anxiety," Kayla said. "My mom uses that word when I get like this. My heart races and my brain tells me to run." Tayla came out of the music room grinning, holding up a thumb, which made everything worse. Kayla's turn was in two minutes. She tried her usual coping trick, the slow breathing the counselor had taught her in the fall, but her mind kept showing her a picture of herself forgetting the words halfway through the second verse.

Mr. Singh was tuning the piano and didn't look up when she came in, which gave her a moment to think. She liked to figure things out, and she had noticed a pattern she couldn't explain: before her last math test she had felt exactly this jittery, and she had gotten the best mark in the class. Before the soccer tryouts, same racing heart, and she had played the sharpest she'd ever played. So maybe, she thought, the feeling wasn't only an enemy. Maybe it was doing something. She decided to test a small idea: instead of fighting the flutters, she would aim them at the song.

"Whenever you're ready," said Mr. Singh. She set the music on the stand, and to her surprise the shaky feeling narrowed into something tight and bright, like a spotlight in her chest. Every word arrived on time. When she hit the high note in the bridge, the one she usually mumbled, it came out clean and sure. She finished and stood there breathing hard, and Mr. Singh said, "That's the most focused I've heard you all year."

In the hallway afterward she told Naomie what she'd worked out. "It's stress," she said. "Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and a short burst of it can actually help you focus, like before a test or a race." Naomie frowned. "Then why does everyone act like it's terrible?" "Because too much of it, for too long, is," Kayla said. "I'm still going to use my coping stuff when it gets bad. This just means I don't have to panic about the panic." Tayla, listening at the door, said she wished she'd known that before her own audition, because she'd spent the whole morning trying to make her nerves go away instead of using them.

The next week Kayla set a boundary for herself, as her mom called it: no practicing past nine o'clock, even when she felt behind, because tired Kayla made careless mistakes and then beat herself up about them. Thursday night at eight fifty-five she closed the piano lid, and when Naomie texted "one more run-through?" she typed back, "No. Tomorrow." On Saturday the cast list went up, and beside the spring solo, in Mr. Singh's neat handwriting, was her name. Naomie pointed at it, and Tayla squeezed her shoulder, and Kayla said, "Okay. Now we get to be nervous about the real thing."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals, and in a street scene they include road edges, curbs and rooflines.
story:
Mr. Zhu set a photograph of an empty street on each desk and tapped the board with a ruler. "Vanishing point," he said, drawing a small dot. "Everything in your street heads there. Draw your orthogonals first." Madison copied the dot onto her paper and then sat still. Orthogonals. The word was new, and she had not been listening when he said which lines counted.

Across the room, Owen had already started. His pencil ran from the bottom edge of his paper straight to the dot, then back down the other side. Madison leaned over. "What are you drawing?" she whispered. "Orthogonals," he said. "Mr. Zhu said them first, so they must matter." She looked at his page. He had drawn two lines and then stopped, chewing his eraser. Rowyn, on her other side, was drawing a curb that angled toward the dot and stopped halfway.

Madison wanted her street to look real, with a shop on one side and a house on the other, and she wanted it before the period ended so Mr. Zhu would hang it beside the emperor print he kept near the window. She studied the photograph instead of guessing. The road's edges ran toward the far distance. So did the curbs. So did the roofs, sloping down toward where the street seemed to shrink away. She picked up her pencil and followed each one with her finger first: road edge, curb, roofline, road edge again. Every one of them, if she extended it in her mind, would land on the same dot.

She drew them in light strokes, all of them, before drawing anything solid. Owen watched her. "Roofs too?" he asked. "Mine only did the road." He erased nothing; he added two rooflines on top of his old lines and shrugged. Rowyn looked at her half-finished curb, extended it, then added a far roofline, and the flat paper began to open up like a corridor. The smell of pencil shavings and damp paper towels filled the room. Mr. Zhu walked the rows and stopped at Madison's desk.

"See?" he said. "Road edges, curbs, rooflines." He pointed at each one with the ruler. "All of them are your orthogonals." Madison nodded and started on the shop, drawing its front face flat and square, then letting its side wall run back toward the dot. The wall behaved. It just worked, like the rule had been there the whole time and she had finally spotted it.

At the end of class Mr. Zhu pinned three streets in a row on the board. Owen's had a road and two roofs. Rowyn's had a curb and a half. Madison's shop sat squarely on its corner with its side sliding back into the distance. "Cumulative effort," Mr. Zhu said. "That's how skill insulates you from panic on the exam." He tapped her roofline last. "Nice line."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: A person's reaction time on a stopwatch is often about a fifth of a second, so timing a longer run makes that error matter less.
story:
Christopher crouched at the top of the ramp in the science room, a marble in his hand, and grinned at Anis across the room. "This time we'll get it. Ball speed, measured like pros." Ms. Sharma had set out ramps, tape measures, stopwatches, and graph paper, and Christopher had been waiting for this lesson all week.

The plan was simple. Roll the ball, time it, measure the distance, divide, and draw a distance-time graph. Elena held stopwatch one at the bottom of the short track. Anis held stopwatch two. Christopher rolled the marble down the ramp and along the floor, and both timers clicked at the same instant, or so it seemed.

"Two point four seconds," Elena announced.

"Two point six," said Anis.

They stared at the stopwatches. Christopher rolled the ball again, and again the numbers disagreed, sometimes by a fifth of a second, sometimes more. "The ball can't take two different amounts of time for the same roll," Christopher said. "Same ramp, same floor, same ball." He walked the track, thinking. He looked at the stopwatches, then at his own thumb, and clicked one a few times. Something was off, and it wasn't the ball.

Then he had it. "It's us. Our reaction time on a stopwatch is often about a fifth of a second. On a short run, that error ruins everything." He said it fast, then heard himself. "So we time a longer run. If the ball rolls farther, the fifth of a second matters less." Elena's eyes went wide. "Let's measure the whole hallway." Ms. Sharma, who had been watering the plants by the window, smiled and said only, "Graphs love long runs."

They moved to the corridor, marked start and finish lines with tape, and stretched the tape measure along the floor. Christopher rolled the marble down the long track. Elena got three point two seconds, Anis got three point two seconds. "The same!" they shouted at once, laughing at the symmetry of the matching numbers. Back in the room, Christopher divided distance by time, plotted the points, and watched a straight line transform his messy afternoon into a clean graph. Anis leaned over his shoulder. "Four point one meters per second. That's a fast marble." Christopher drew one more line through the points and tapped the end of it. "That's the speed. That's it, right there."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Loaded words carry strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd "protesters" or "rioters" can push readers toward opposite opinions.
story:
Charlie had the living room to herself until five o'clock, which meant the coffee table, the laptop, and both remotes were hers. Mr. Suryanto's assignment was due Monday: find two news stories about the same event and figure out what made them feel different. Leana and Magalie were coming over at four, and Charlie wanted to have something ready before they arrived, because she was tired of being the one who showed up unprepared.

She found the first headline fast. It said thousands of protesters filled the square, peaceful and determined. The photo showed people holding signs, one little girl with a paper cup of juice that had probably once held nectar from a juice cart, the kind of small detail that made the scene feel warm and almost tranquil. Charlie read it twice and felt her chest go tight with sympathy. Whoever these people were, they sounded brave.

Then she opened the second site, and her stomach dropped. This headline said a mob of rioters rampaged through the same square. The photo showed the same plaza, the same fountain, even what looked like the same little girl, except now the caption said she was fleeing the chaos. Charlie sat very still. Same day, same place, same crowd. She scrolled back and forth between the tabs so many times the touchpad grew warm under her finger.

She grabbed a sticky note and wrote the two words side by side. Protesters. Rioters. She said each one out loud in the quiet living room and noticed that her own face changed, softening at the first and hardening at the second. It was like the words had feelings packed inside them, feelings that had nothing to do with what actually happened. The crowd itself was invisible to her; she couldn't see it, couldn't know it. All she had was the wrapping.

When Leana and Magalie arrived, Charlie said nothing at first. She let Leana read headline one and Magalie read headline two, watching their faces. Leana sighed with admiration. Magalie muttered that the people should be arrested. Then Charlie turned the laptop so they could see both tabs together, and the room went silent except for the aquarium filter humming by the window.

"Read them again," Charlie said. "Same square. Same fountain. Same day."

Leana leaned close, then closer, then sat back hard against the couch cushions. "They're describing the same crowd, and one calls them protesters and one calls them rioters."

"And I believed both," Magalie said quietly. She pulled out her notebook. "Okay. We should prioritize this for our project. This is the whole thing."

They spent the next hour finding more pairs, hunched over the coffee table, arguing about which words were doing the pushing. At some point Magalie's mom called and she ignored the phone. "Look at this one," she said, tapping the screen. "Same story, third site. They just call them 'the crowd.'"

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: The formula =SUM(B2:B10) adds every cell from B2 to B10; the colon between the two cells marks a range.
story:
Ms. Ahmed had agreed to let the Computer Club run a pretend lemonade stand in the cafeteria, as long as the money was fake and nobody actually drank anything. Alice was in charge of the spreadsheet, which would have been fine except that she had written the week's sales into cells B2 through B10 and then, on Friday, added them up with a calculator and her finger on the screen.

"Forty-one dollars and fifty cents," she announced. Veronika, who had been guarding the pretend cash box, which was actually a pencil case, looked doubtful.

"That's not the currency we're using," Veronika said. "Sandra priced everything in pretend dollars. Where did you get cents?"

Alice checked the paper order form. Sandra had sold a "premium half-cup" for fifty pretend cents on Thursday, apparently to a fourth-grader who did not question the concept. So the total might be right, but Alice had counted nine rows on the screen and the calculator said she had added only eight numbers. Somewhere a sale had slipped past her finger.

She scrolled up and down the column. B2, B3, B4, all the way to B10, a tidy little fence of numbers. She knew the computer could add. She had watched Ms. Ahmed demonstrate a pie chart on Monday using data about the school's lost-and-found socks, which was a whole other problem. There had to be a way to make the machine do the counting for her, so it couldn't drop a cell the way her finger did.

In the empty cell at the bottom, she typed =SUM(B2:B10) and pressed enter. The number 41.5 appeared instantly. She tried it again with a smaller range to make sure she understood, typing =SUM(B2:B3), and got only the first two sales, six dollars. The colon, she realized, marked a range, everything from B2 all the way to B10, no finger required.

"Veronika, it got all nine," she said. "The colon between the two cells is the range. I don't even have to look at the middle ones."

"I don't look at the middle ones either," Veronika said. "That's why Sandra is in charge of the premium half-cup."

Alice highlighted the column, clicked the bar chart button, and watched nine bars spring up, Thursday's fifty-cent bar looking small and porous, like it might not hold together under questioning. She printed it and taped it to the table.

Ms. Ahmed walked by, studied the chart, and pointed at the short bar. "I'd like to meet this customer," she said.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: To test whether n is prime, you only need to try divisors up to its square root, because if n is a times b, one of them is no bigger than that root.
story:
Eli sat cross-legged on his bedroom floor with the laptop balanced on a stack of comics, typing his first prime checker. Mr. Martínez had shown the class the basics on Friday, and Eli wanted to beat Wilson and Yousif to a working program by Monday. His code asked for a number, then tried dividing it by every number from two up to n minus one, printing "prime" if nothing divided it. He tested it on 7, then 31, then 97, and it answered instantly. He leaned back, grinning, and snapped a photo of the screen for the group chat.

Wilson replied first. "Cool. Try 999,999,937." Eli rolled his eyes, typed it in, and pressed enter. The cursor blinked. He waited. It kept blinking. He got up, drank some water, came back, and the cursor was still blinking, the fan inside the laptop whirring like it was trying to take off. "That's not a bug," he muttered. "That's just slow." But slow felt like a different problem, and he couldn't see the cause of it anywhere on the screen.

Yousif called him. "Mine's stuck too. Wilson's laughing at us. He says his finished in under a second." In the background Wilson's voice carried, that infectious giggle that made even teachers smile, though right now it only made Eli's jaw tighten. "He's going to ridicule us in class all week," Yousif said. "My mom says don't crack your knuckles, you'll wreck the cartilage, and I'm cracking them like crazy."

"Wait," Eli said slowly. He grabbed a pencil and his math notebook. Wilson's program was different. Wilson had mentioned something offhand in the chat, a line about a square root, and Eli hadn't paid attention. He wrote Wilson's number at the top of the page and stared at it. If a number is a times b, he thought, then those two factors multiply to make the whole thing. One of them has to be the small one. He chewed the pencil end, drew arrows, crossed out three wrong ideas, and then went very still.

"You only need to try divisors up to the square root of n," he said out loud, mostly to himself, "because if n is a times b, one of them is no bigger than that root." He said it again, faster. Every factor pair had a small member, and the small one lived below the square root, so nothing past it could sneak in without a partner he'd already found. Yousif said, "Say that again," and Eli repeated it while typing, changing his loop so it stopped at the square root instead of marching almost to n itself.

He typed 999,999,937 and pressed enter. The fan was still whirring from before, the room hot and quiet, and he held his breath the way he did before a free throw. The answer appeared before the fan had time to slow down. "prime," the screen said. Eli whooped so loudly his dad yelled from the kitchen to ask what was on fire. He took a screenshot, sent it to the chat, and typed, "Wilson. Race me on something bigger."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
The portable grill had taken twenty minutes to light, and Nicholas was starting to think the chicken would take twenty more. Around the campsite the shadows of the pines had stretched long across the picnic table, and his dad had said they would be back from the canoe put-in by sundown, hungry. That gave him maybe forty minutes. His sister, Sarah, sat on the cooler with a flashlight she kept clicking on and off, which did not help.

"You keep staring at it," she said. "Staring doesn't cook chicken."

"I'm not staring. I'm thinking." The pieces looked done on the outside, golden and striped dark from the grate. But at home his dad always said looks could fool you, and Nicholas had watched him slide a thin metal probe into a roast once without explaining why. In the plastic bin of camp cooking gear, under the tongs and the roll of foil, Nicholas had found a food thermometer with a dial like a tiny clock. He had carried it in his pocket all afternoon, and now he wiped it off and pushed the tip into the thickest part of the biggest piece.

The needle climbed and stopped at 150.

"Is that good?" Sarah asked, leaning over. She smelled like bug spray and kettle corn.

"I don't know yet. But it's not done now, whatever done is." Nicholas thought about the number as he closed the grill lid. Somewhere in the back of his mind was a fact from a poster in the school kitchen, something about poultry and a number, and the more he turned it over, the more coherent it became: 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured in the thickest part. That was the rule. Not the color of the juices, not how the surface looked. The number was the thing that mattered, and the thermometer was the only way to read it.

He gave the chicken five minutes and tested again. 158. The needle was creeping up in small honest steps. To pass the time he poured lemonade from the big blue vessel they used as a pitcher, and Sarah held the cups steady while he poured without spilling. A raccoon watched them from the edge of the fire ring, unafraid, until Sarah shooed it off.

"What's the needle for?" she asked, pointing at the dial.

"The numbers signify temperature," Nicholas said. "Wherever the needle points, that's how hot the chicken is right there."

At the third test the needle swung past 160 and settled at 167. Nicholas held the thermometer up to the last light so he could be sure. The thickest piece had passed 165, so the others, which were smaller and had been on the same heat, would be there too. He moved everything to a clean plate and covered it with foil.

Headlights swept across the trees, and the truck doors slammed. His dad came up the path first, sniffing the air. "Is that dinner, or did we imagine it?"

Nicholas lifted the foil so he could see. "It's chicken, and it hit 167 in the middle."

His dad picked up the thermometer from the table, turned it over in his hand, and smiled. "You checked it the right way, then." He reached for a plate as Sarah started pouring lemonade all around.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: The sense of smell naturally declines in old age, a change called presbyosmia.
story:
The problem started on Tuesday morning, when the kitchen filled with smoke and Grandpa just sat there reading the paper. George came running, waving a towel at the shrieking smoke detector, and found the toast black as charcoal. "Grandpa, didn't you smell it burning?" His grandfather looked up, blinking at the haze. "Smell what?"

That afternoon George's grandpa, who was staying for the whole week, wanted to go to the Saturday market to buy spices for his famous chili. George liked the market, with its crates of peppers and the stall where a man sold honey in dusty jars, but he couldn't stop thinking about the toast. Grandpa had also eaten a sandwich with cheese that had gone off, and had put way too much onion in the soup without noticing. Something was going on, and it wasn't carelessness.

At the market, Grandpa picked up a jar of cumin, opened it, and sniffed. "Smells strong," he declared. George took a sniff himself and almost coughed. The jar was fenugreek, and it smelled sharp enough to sting. He said nothing at first, but as they walked past the flower stall he watched his grandfather bury his nose in a bunch of lavender and shrug. A woman beside them sighed with pleasure at the same flowers. That was the pattern. Other people smelled things strongly. Grandpa smelled almost nothing.

George had an idea, and he decided to test it right there between the vegetable stall and the bread stand. "Grandpa, close your eyes," he said. "I'll hold something up, and you tell me what it is." He grabbed a lemon, a bar of soap from the craft table, and a cinnamon bun. Grandpa got the soap, sort of, after a long pause, but he couldn't tell lemon from bun, and he mixed up the soap with the lemon too. "Well," Grandpa said, opening his eyes, "that's that, then."

When they got home, George looked it up on the library computer while Grandpa rested. He found it fast: the sense of smell naturally declines in old age. There was even a word for it. He copied it onto his hand.

At dinner, George showed Grandpa what he'd written. "Presbyosmia," Grandpa read slowly. Then he laughed, a real laugh. "So the chili needs a taste tester." He pointed his spoon at George. "You're hired." After that, they cooked together every night, George sniffing and tasting while Grandpa adjusted the seasonings, calling out instructions like a coach. The chili won second prize at the market's fall contest, and the judge said its flavor was distinct, one you could pick out from across the room.

The week before he left, Grandpa put a new smoke detector right outside the kitchen door. "One for you," he said, tapping it, "and this one's for me." Then he handed George a jar of cumin, the real one this time, and George unscrewed the lid and took a long, careful breath.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Desert rainfall is not just low but unreliable: a desert may go years with almost no rain and then get a heavy downpour in a single storm.
story:
The rental car smelled like sunscreen and pretzels when Hudson spotted the first yellow sign: WARNING, FLOOD RISK AREA. They were in the middle of a desert, hours from anything green, and the road outside was so dry it had cracked like old paint. "Flood signs in a desert," he said. "That's like putting a shark warning in a cow pasture." Rebecca, wedged beside him with her notebook of climate graphs, snickered without looking up.

Rebecca wanted an A on their climate project, and she'd brought two printed graphs to prove she deserved it: one for a rainforest, one for this desert. The rainforest graph looked like a comb, with tidy bars of rainfall every single month. The desert graph looked like a mouth missing most of its teeth. "See," she said, tapping it, "my graph shows the rainforest gets rain every month, all year. The desert gets almost nothing." Hudson frowned at the desert's lopsided spikes. Almost nothing, except one tall bar that stood alone like a flagpole. He remembered, suddenly, the trip two summers ago, when his uncle had recounted the story of a canyon flash flood, how a wall of water had roared through on a day with not a single cloud overhead. Hudson had thought the man was exaggerating back then. Now he wasn't so sure.

"Wait," Hudson said. He pulled out a marker and drew a dotted line on Rebecca's graph, connecting the empty years to that one spike. "What if the desert doesn't just get less rain? What if it's unreliable? Like, years with almost no rain at all, and then one storm dumps a whole bunch at once." Rebecca tilted her head. "That would explain the flood signs." "It would explain the flood signs," Hudson agreed, and they grinned at each other the way you do when a mystery cracks open in the back seat.

At the next gas stop, Mr. Chea, their neighbor and the official driver of this expedition, went in for coffee while Hudson studied a poster by the register. It showed a dry wash with a phone number and the words: REPORT YOUR RAIN SIGHTINGS. YOUR TESTIMONY HELPS US WARN OTHERS. While he waited, Hudson texted his dad, who was stuck at home working: "You will not believe this. Desert flood warnings are real. Not subjective opinion. Scientific fact, with graphs." His dad sent back a single message: "Then why did Mr. Chea pack an umbrella? Check the trunk."

Hudson lifted the trunk lid. There, folded beside the jumper cables, sat a compact umbrella, looking smug. He held it up as Mr. Chea came out jingling his keys. "Expecting a flood, Mr. Chea?" Mr. Chea took the umbrella, popped it open over his head in the blazing sun, and walked back to the car like a dignified beetle. "Insurance," he said. On the horizon, a single gray cloud was beginning to stack itself up.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: In Mexican tradition, a quinceañera, the celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday, usually begins with a Mass of thanksgiving.
story:
The backyard smelled of grilled corn and cinnamon, and Gavin's cousin Rosario kept disappearing behind the garage with a folded paper in her fist. At the long table under the string lights, their grandmother was telling everyone that a quinceañera, the celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday, usually begins with a Mass of thanksgiving, which was why Rosario had to stand up in front of the whole church and deliver a reading. Gavin watched his cousin slump in her chair, poking at her rice, looking lethargic in a way that had nothing to do with being tired.

"Want me to quiz you?" he asked, following her behind the garage with two paper plates of flan.

"I freeze," Rosario said. "I know it at home, then I open my mouth in front of people and it's gone." She read the line aloud again, flawless and quick, then groaned. "See? Alone I'm fine."

Gavin chewed and thought about that. At home the words came; in front of people they vanished. So the problem wasn't the words, it was the eyes on her, which meant practicing the words alone was like practicing swimming on dry grass. He remembered last summer, when he'd had to recite a poem for Mr. Hughes's class and had bombed it in front of thirty kids. Afterward, his mother had made him perform it three times for the family in the kitchen, and by the third time his voice had stopped shaking, because the scary part had been the audience, and he had gotten used to one.

"Okay, new plan," Gavin said. "Don't practice alone. Practice on us." He dragged two lawn chairs into the space behind the garage and set them facing the paper-plate "congregation." "Every time you finish, the crowd gets flan." Rosario laughed, but she stood, spread her feet like she was bracing against wind, and began. She stumbled on the second line. He made her start over. She stumbled again. He waved the flan like a bribe.

By the fourth try, the words stopped hiding. When Rosario inhaled before the last sentence, Gavin noticed she wasn't staring at the paper anymore, she was looking over his head at the fence, steady as a fence post. "One more," she said, "with everybody." She marched around to the yard, where the aunts and the little cousins were still eating, and climbed onto the low wall by the grill.

"Attention, consumers of my grandmother's cooking," she announced, and the whole table turned. She began the reading, slow and clear, her voice carrying past the corn smoke to the dark edge of the yard. When she finished, their grandmother was already on her feet.

"Again," Grandma said, wiping her eyes with the corner of her apron. "And louder."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Smokey Bear's campfire rule is drown, stir, drown again, then feel for heat, because if a campfire is too hot to touch, it is too hot to leave.
story:
Bennett had been at Camp Tamarack for exactly four hours, and already the dining hall smelled like burnt oatmeal and bug spray. He sat at the end of a long table with his cabin group, tray untouched, listening to Iyla from Cabin 6 argue that the morning's campfire had been left perfectly safe.

"It was out," she said. "Gray ash, no flames. Done."

"Then why did Mr. Singh make everyone go back?" Bennett asked.

Iyla shrugged. "He likes bossing people around."

Lisa leaned across the table. "He made them pour water on it twice. And stir it with a shovel. Then pour again. My brother was in that group last year."

Bennett turned that over. Pour, stir, pour. That was a rule, not a mood. Mr. Singh was making the whole group redo something they thought was finished, which meant the counselor believed a fire could look dead and not be dead. That was a hidden cause, invisible, the kind of thing you couldn't settle by staring at it. You'd have to test it somehow.

After lunch, Bennett found Mr. Singh stacking cups behind the counter. "How do you actually know when a campfire is out?"

Mr. Singh looked at him for a second. "You feel for heat with the back of your hand. If it's too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave."

That was the whole answer, and it had a comparison built into it, one Bennett filed away. He walked back to the tables thinking about the camp's evening skit, which his cabin was supposed to perform at the Friday campfire. They'd been arguing all morning about which skit to do, and Mr. Singh had finally made them vote by ballot, folded papers and all, because Iyla refused to yield on her talking-squirrel idea. Iyla had also announced that a campfire skit would be impossible now, since Mr. Singh was clearly going to ban campfires forever after the morning's disaster.

Bennett had voted for Iyla's skit anyway, mostly because the other option was forty minutes of knock-knock jokes. He found her by the juice machine.

"If the fire gets a total ban," she said, "we do the skit in here. In the dining hall. Around the ketchup."

"Mr. Singh isn't banning anything," Bennett said. "He's just making sure the fire is actually cold before anyone leaves it. That's all it was. You pour water on it, stir it, pour again, then feel for heat with the back of your hand. Too hot to touch means too hot to leave."

Iyla chewed on that. She'd spent four hours believing the counselors had invented a punishment just for her group, and the simpler explanation, that the fire had only looked dead, was somehow more annoying. "Fine," she said. "Skit at the fire. But I'm checking it myself first. Back of my hand."

Friday night came, and the fire burned down to coals while the squirrels delivered their punchlines. When the crowd filed out, Iyla stayed behind, cup in hand. She poured, stirred with the shovel, poured again, then hovered her hand over the ash.

"Cold," she announced, sounding almost disappointed.

Bennett held out his own hand anyway, and she smacked it away. "Back of the hand only," she said. "House rules."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Each operation has an inverse that undoes it: subtraction undoes addition, and division undoes multiplication.
story:
The bell over the door clattered as Alexandra pushed into Mr. Ma's corner store, her math worksheet folded into a sad square in her back pocket. Eli was already at the counter, sliding coins across the glass for a bag of chips. "You look like somebody stole your bike," Eli said. "Worse," Alexandra said. "Homework. x plus 7 equals 12, and about eight more just like it. I keep guessing numbers and most of them are wrong."

Mr. Ma, restocking the drink cooler, glanced over. "Guessing is a parasite," he said. "It eats your time and gives nothing back." Alexandra blinked at him, then laughed a little despite herself. "That's what guessing feels like," she admitted. "But I don't know what else to do."

She spread the worksheet on the counter between the lottery machine and a rack of beef jerky. Eli leaned in, chewing. "Okay, so the x is hiding behind the plus 7," Alexandra said slowly, tapping the equation with her pencil. "I can't see it. But something has to undo the plus 7." She thought about the numbers Mr. Ma kept in his head all day, how he balanced every customer's change. "If somebody adds 7 to a pile, the only thing that takes the pile back is subtracting 7."

"So take 7 away from the 12," Eli said. She wrote it. 12 minus 7 was 5, so x had to be 5. She checked it the way she'd check change: 5 plus 7 made 12. It worked. "Wait," she said, heart quickening. "Subtraction undoes addition." She looked down the page at the next one, 3x equals 15, and stopped cold. "Different problem. Adding isn't involved here." She stared at it, then at the three bags of chips Eli had bought with the same amount of money, three times over. "If multiplying by 3 built it," she said, "then dividing by 3 has to unbuild it." She divided 15 by 3 and got 5 again. Both answers were 5, which felt almost like a magic trick, except it wasn't.

She worked the rest standing at the counter while Mr. Ma rang up a customer, being systematic about it, asking each time what operation had been done and what its inverse would be. She got one wrong, 4x plus 2 equals 18, because she divided first and got a mess of decimals, and Mr. Ma said nothing, just waited while she stared at it. "The plus 2 is in the way," she muttered. "Get rid of that first, then the times 4." She subtracted 2 from both sides, then divided both sides by 4, and the hiding number stepped out clean. She folded the worksheet, no longer a sad square but a neat rectangle, and bought a bag of chips with her last coins.

"So you conquered it?" Eli asked on the sidewalk outside. Alexandra held up the bag, tore it open, and said, "Every single one."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average, an effect known as home advantage.
story:
Cameron had lost every away game so far this season, six of them, and he was starting to take it personally. Today the Hawks were finally back at Riverside Park, on their own patchy field with the goal net his dad had helped restring, and Cameron meant to figure something out before kickoff.

"Watch the other team," he told Casey while they laced up their cleats near the water fountain. Casey was new this year and still got nervous before games, so Cameron handed her the spare shin guards he kept in his bag, the synthetic ones that dried fast. "I think there's a pattern to why we keep losing on the road and doing okay here. I want to test it."

"Test it how?" Casey asked.

"Coach keeps saying home teams win more than half their games on average," Cameron said. "It's called home advantage. I'm going to count. If it's real, it should show up in more than just our team." He had spent the week writing down the results of every park league game on the schedule pinned to the snack shack, and the numbers leaned one direction, toward the home side, game after game.

The first half was rough. The other team's big midfielder barrelled through like a runaway truck, and Cameron got knocked flat so hard it felt like his intestines had been rearranged.
