He lay in the grass for a second, embarrassed, before Will hauled him up by the wrist. "You okay?" Will asked, already waving toward the sideline where Ms. Takahashi, the rec leader, was holding the water bottle ready. Cameron nodded, drank, and got back in position.

In the second half, things shifted. Cameron noticed their opponents kept looking to their bench for instructions, because they couldn't hear their coach over the playground noise, while the Hawks ran their plays from memory. He didn't know if that was part of the pattern or not, and he didn't care to guess. He just played. When the ball spun loose in front of the net, he trapped it, turned, and shot low into the corner, and the keeper never moved. Three home games, three home wins.

After the whistle, Cameron added the result to his notebook and showed Casey the tally. "Still more than half," he said. "Every week." Casey grinned and bumped his shoulder with hers. Will jogged over, holding out the ball. "Same time next Saturday?"

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Earth's tilt slowly varies between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees over a cycle of about 41,000 years.
story:
Vincent had exactly forty minutes to figure out the seasons before his group presented at the museum's demonstration table, and so far all he knew was that summer existed, which felt like thin material for a science talk.

"Maybe it's distance from the sun," said Maverick, bouncing a plastic globe on his palm like a basketball. "We get closer, we cook."

"Then why is it winter in Australia while we're swimming?" said Ariya, who had already claimed the flashlight for the demonstration and was refusing to give it up. She aimed the beam at the ceiling and made a light saber noise.

Vincent took the globe and stabbed a finger at its middle. "Okay, so if distance is out, it's this tilt thing. The Earth leans." He tilted the globe sideways, held the flashlight steady, and watched the light smear across the northern half. More light on one half meant more heat, and less on the other meant less. That was it. That was the whole seasons puzzle, hiding where nobody could actually see it, out in space. He spun the globe around the flashlight, keeping the tilt pointed the same direction the whole way around, and the bright half switched sides halfway through the orbit. Winter became summer became winter again. He grinned so hard his cheeks hurt.

The demonstration went better than expected until the museum educator, Ms. Tremblay, dropped by and asked the question that broke everything. "Nice work. Now, what would happen if Earth leaned more than it does?"

Maverick immediately said, "More extreme seasons, obviously," and Vincent, wanting to sound equally obvious, said, "Sure, and the tilt never changes anyway, so who cares."

Ms. Tremblay raised one eyebrow in a way that made Vincent's stomach drop. She walked him to a display near the planetarium door, where a small brass plaque sat under a magnifying lens so visitors could read the tiny print. Vincent leaned in and read it twice, because the first time he was sure he'd imagined it. Earth's tilt wasn't fixed. It slowly varied between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees, over a cycle of about 41,000 years.

"Forty-one thousand years," Vincent said out loud. "So it's basically leaning back and forth, just so slowly that nobody notices."

"Sloth tilt," said Ariya, who had followed them over. "The laziest wobble in the universe."

Vincent ran back to the demonstration table, snatched the globe, and grabbed a stirring stick from the supply bin to tape against its axis, then bent it a few degrees further. "Ms. Tremblay, we can simulate it. Watch, this is Earth leaning more." He orbited the globe around Ariya's flashlight. The bright patch on the tilted half shrank smaller and the dark half stretched wider than before, like the seasons were arguing louder. "When it leans more, summers and winters get more intense. When it leans less, they get milder. It's still doing it right now, just at sloth speed."

Ms. Tremblay crouched to eye level with the globe. "So tell me, presenter, which way is it leaning in our lifetime?"

"Doesn't matter," Vincent said. "By the time it changes enough to notice, we'll all be fossils." The group laughed, even Maverick, who was now trying to balance the globe on one finger and turning the whole table into something turbulent and dangerous.

"Steady," Ariya said, holding the flashlight out like a traffic cop. "Nobody orbits until Vincent says go."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Seedlings grown indoors are usually hardened off, set outside for a little longer each day, so they can adjust to sun and wind before planting.
story:
Isabelle had been growing tomato seedlings on the kitchen windowsill since March, and by the last week of school they were taller than her hand, with leaves like small green stars. Her ambition was a whole vegetable garden in the backyard: tomatoes, beans, lettuce, everything. On Saturday morning she carried the pots outside, dug holes along the fence, and planted every seedling in the warm soil. "You're home," she told them, and patted the dirt.

By noon the tomato leaves had gone soft and floppy, drooping against their own stems. Isabelle knelt in the grass and stared. She had watered them. She hadn't dug them up wrong; the roots looked fine when they went in. The sky was clear and bright, and she sat there squinting up at it, wondering.

Her friend Axton came over after lunch, drawn by the promise of lemonade, and crouched beside the wilted row. "They look sad," he said. "Maybe they need more water." But the soil was already damp, and Isabelle kept coming back to the same thought: the seedlings had spent their whole lives behind glass. Her grandmother's seedlings, the ones she'd seen at the farm stand, sat outside in flats on a table, day after day, before anyone bought them. There was a pattern there, and she wanted to test it.

She ran inside, found her one remaining seedling, the runt she'd never planted, and set it on the porch steps in the sun. She watched it for ten minutes. Its leaves began to droop too, right there in the pot, with perfect roots, untouched by her shovel. So it wasn't the planting. It was the outdoors itself, the sun and the moving air, that the indoor plants weren't ready for.

Her neighbor Mr. Foster was washing his car across the fence, and he glanced over at the row of drooping tomatoes. "Got eager, did you," he called. "Those need to be hardened off. You set them out a little longer each day, and they toughen up." Isabelle stood very still, holding the runt in its pot. "A little longer each day," she repeated, and he nodded and went back to his hubcap.

So she got to work. She gave the wilted seedlings shade with an old sheet propped on chairs, and each morning she moved the sheet so the plants got a bit more light, a bit more wind, for a bit longer. The floppy stems lifted first, then the leaves. When the beans she'd planted straight from seed pushed up through the soil, they stood firm and green in full sun from their very first hour, because they'd never known anything else.

Axton came by a week later and squinted at the garden. "They're standing up," he said. Isabelle watered the row, careful not to splash the leaves, and set the little runt, still in its pot, out on the edge of the fence in the brightest spot of the afternoon. "One more hour," she told it, "then you go in the ground."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Many school pools are 25 yards or 25 meters long, called short course, while Olympic swimming races are held in 50-meter pools, called long course.
story:
Amelia stood at the edge of the school pool with her tryout card in her hand, staring at the number the coach had written there. Fifty-eight seconds for two lengths. Last summer, at the big municipal pool, she had swum two lengths in fifty-six seconds, and she had walked into the gym that morning certain she would beat that time. Now she wondered what had gone wrong. Was she slower? Was she tired? Or was something else going on?

Jules leaned over the lane rope, dripping. "Fifty-eight's good. That'll make the team."

"It doesn't make sense," Amelia said. "I was faster at the other pool. I counted my strokes, and I counted the same today." She looked down the lane, at the turquoise water, the smell of chlorine sharp in her nose, the tiles blurring under the surface. Two pools, two different numbers for the same swim. Were the two pools even the same?

She remembered standing at the municipal pool in August, her toes curled on the rough deck, counting the flags along the ceiling to keep from being nervous. The lifeguard had said something that day, and it came back to her now: that pool was built for real races, the kind she watched on television. The lanes there had gone on and on, like rivers. This school pool felt small enough to cross in a few breaths.

"Ulysse," she called down the deck, "how long is the school pool?"

He shrugged. "Twenty-five yards." He pointed at a faded sign above the diving blocks, its letters greenish like lichen on a rock. "Says so right there."

Amelia walked to the deep end and back, counting her steps, and the pieces began to fit together like a puzzle she had been holding upside down. At the municipal pool she had swum one length and back, and it had taken her fifty-six seconds. One length there was twice as long as one length here. Two lengths of the big pool was a longer race than two lengths of this one. Her times weren't the same race at all; they didn't correspond. If the big pool was fifty meters, then her summer swim had covered more water in less time, which meant she was actually faster now, not slower. She thought of dinosaurs, extinct and gone, and laughed at herself. Her slow-time theory had just gone extinct too.

She ran to the coach's table. "The school pool is twenty-five yards, so it's short course, right? And the Olympic one is fifty meters. That's called long course."

The coach looked up from her clipboard. "That's right. You can't compare times between them."

"Then can I write that next to my fifty-eight?" Amelia asked, already reaching for the pencil. "So nobody thinks I got slower?"

"Go ahead," the coach said, and Amelia printed it in small, careful letters, then jumped back into the warm water for her next heat.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Distracting, such as changing the subject or starting a new game, can interrupt teasing without challenging the teaser directly.
story:
Dominic had been waiting for Sky's birthday party all week, and the second he walked through the door he spotted the bouncy castle in the backyard, the table of arcade prizes, and Arvin, standing alone near the snack table while two kids from another school circled him like seagulls around fries.

"Nice glasses, four-eyes," one of them said. "Can you even see through those things?"

Dominic's stomach tightened. He wanted to shout at them, but shouting had backfired in fourth grade when he'd yelled at a teaser on the bus and made everything worse; the kid had just gotten louder, and the teased kid had gotten teased for needing a bodyguard. So he stood there, holding his gift bag, thinking hard. Why did teasers keep going? Because they liked the audience, he decided. The whole room was watching Arvin, and the two kids were performing. If the audience looked somewhere else, would the show stop?

He needed to test it. He scanned the room. In the kitchen, Sky's dad was pulling a giant sheet cake out of the fridge, candles still in a box beside it. Dominic took a breath and marched to the middle of the party.

"Everybody!" he called. "They're cutting the cake, like, right now! Come on!"

The whole room turned. Kids stampeded toward the kitchen, and the unanimous rush of sneakers on the tile swallowed everything else. Even the two teasers jogged over, suddenly more interested in frosting than in Arvin. Dominic hung back, and Arvin drifted over to stand beside him, pretending to inspect a poster of the solar system on the wall.

"Thanks," Arvin said quietly. "You didn't have to do that."

Dominic shrugged, though inside he felt like he'd won a prize. "I just changed the subject. Distraction. It works better than yelling at them, I think."

Sky appeared with two plates of cake, thundering over like a small storm. "Did you see that cake? My dad spent an hour installing the candles, he had to use this special holder thing for the number eleven, it goes right down the spine of the cake, all eleven candles in a row." She handed them each a fork. "Best one yet, right?"

"Definitely," Arvin said, and it was the first full sentence he'd said all afternoon.

Later, out in the bouncy castle, the two teasers tried again. One of them pointed at Arvin's glasses and opened his mouth, and Dominic, mid-bounce, didn't even look at them. He just launched into the biggest cannonball of his life, and the whole castle wobbled like jelly. Every kid shrieked and scrambled to copy him, and by the time the bouncing settled, the teasers had bounced away to the other side.

Arvin caught Dominic's eye and grinned. "Cannonball distraction," he said. "You're getting good at this."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of children's bones, are weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress.
story:
The gym smelled like rubber and floor wax, and Mackenzie's left knee had started aching again by the second drill. It was a strange ache, always in the same spot, just below the kneecap, and it showed up halfway through every practice lately. She glanced down at her legs. Both knees looked symmetrical, same shape, same scrapes, but only the left one complained.

At water break she found Lexa by the bleachers. "Does your knee ever hurt? Like, right here?" Mackenzie pressed the spot below her own kneecap.

"After jump rope day, sometimes," Lexa said. "Why?"

Mackenzie didn't answer right away. She was counting in her head. Last week they had done two hundred jumps, then layups, then box jumps. The week before, almost the same. The ache never came on game days, when they jumped less and rested more. It came after the practices with the most repetitions. "I think it's not random," she said slowly. "I think it's the amount."

"Amount of what?"

"Jumping. Same thing every time. Like a pattern."

Lexa shrugged. "Tell Coach."

Instead, Mackenzie tried an experiment on herself. At the next practice, when Ms. Nowak set up the box jump station, Mackenzie did half the reps everyone else did and spent the extra time working on her passing. If the jumping was the hidden cause, the ache should stay away. By the end of the hour, her knee was quiet for the first time in three weeks. She felt something loosen in her chest, though she also felt a little guilty, like she'd been keeping a secret.

She hadn't been the only one watching reps. Markus, who wanted the starting point guard spot more than he wanted lunch some days, had been hoarding the ball all season, taking extra shooting drills after everyone left. Today his right elbow was wrapped in ice, and he sat on the bench while the scrimmage ran without him. Mackenzie sat down beside him.

"What happened?"

"Youth league baseball, last spring," Markus said. "I was a pitcher. Coach made me stop mid-game because I'd hit my pitch limit for the day. I thought it was so unfair. Then the doctor said my growth plates were still open." He shifted the ice pack. "Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of kids' bones. They're weaker than the bone around them. That's why they put limits on young athletes, all that repetitive stress." He looked at the court. "I kept shooting anyway this season. Now my elbow's the one saying stop."

Mackenzie told him about her knee, and the half-reps, and how the ache had vanished. "I was going to keep testing it," she said. "Two more practices, half the jumps, see if the pattern holds. But maybe I should just tell Ms. Nowak."

"Tell her," Markus said. "I wish I'd told somebody in April."

The scrimmage ended, and Ms. Nowak walked over with her clipboard. Mackenzie stood up, knees wobbling just a little, and said, "Coach, can I talk to you about the jump drills?"

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was started in 1967 by John van Hengel.
story:
The sign at the front of the Pinewood Residence read "Community Food Bank, Tuesdays 3 to 6," and Ella stood outside it for a full minute before she went in. Her mother had signed her up for volunteering without asking, which felt arbitrary, like being assigned a seat on a bus she hadn't chosen to board. Inside, folding tables ran down the lounge, and Ms. Georgiou, who ran the distribution, handed her a clipboard and an apron before she could even say hello.

"You'll stock shelves, then help the residents choose," Ms. Georgiou said. "Ask before you assume what anyone wants."

Layton from her science class was already there, stacking cans of soup with Khaled, who had apparently volunteered all last year and knew everyone by name. Ella was put on the far table, the one with bread and fruit, and for the first hour it was simple: smile, offer, bag. But she noticed something odd. Almost every resident from the third floor turned down the oranges, while the second-floor residents took them eagerly. By four o'clock the pattern was so steady she started keeping count on the back of a receipt.

"Maybe the third floor just hates vitamin C," Layton joked when she mentioned it.

Eella didn't think so. She remembered Khaled saying the third-floor hallway had been repainted last month, and she had a hunch. During a lull, she carried a small basket upstairs, asked the nurse at the desk, and tested it: the orange scent saturated the third-floor corridor, mingling with paint fumes so strongly that several residents had gone off citrus entirely. The rule she'd guessed was real. Nobody hated oranges. Their hallway was simply doing something to their appetites that nobody down in the lounge could see.

When she came back down, she switched tactics. She offered the third-floor residents apples and bananas first, and she moved the orange bin nearer the door, where the smell could fade before people reached the tables. Within an hour, the third floor was taking fruit again, and Mrs. Abery, who had waved the oranges away twice, put two apples in her bag and said, "Smart girl. I couldn't stand the smell, but I didn't like to say."

In the break room afterward, Ella found a framed poster on the wall while she waited for the kettle. It told the story of the very first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, started in 1967 by a man named John van Hengel. She read it twice, then carried her tea out to where Khaled was wiping tables.

"Did you know this whole idea started with one guy?" she said. "John van Hengel, 1967, Phoenix, Arizona. The first one ever was St. Mary's Food Bank."

Khaled nodded. "That poster's why half of us volunteer here. Somebody had to start it."

Ella looked at her clipboard, at the tally marks she'd made, at the empty orange bin by the door. Somebody had to start noticing things too. She wrote "third floor: fruit near door" on the sign-in sheet for next Tuesday, and Ms. Georgiou, reading over her shoulder, circled it and pinned it to the corkboard.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: A red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion, so not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing.
story:
Tristan slid the short story packet across the table in the back corner of Bellweather Books, where the Saturday book club met between the poetry shelf and a cardboard cutout of a detective dog. "I figured it out," he said. "The umbrella in paragraph two is foreshadowing. When Mrs. Vale carries it on a sunny day, it means the flood is coming at the end."

Elisha tapped her copy. "That's what I thought too. But Mr. Holloway said to be careful."

"Careful of what?"

She pointed at a line near the bottom of page one, where the gardener mentions a locked boathouse. "Chase says the boathouse is the real clue. He bet a cookie the thief hides there."

Chase arrived late, cookie already in hand, and dropped into the chair beside Tristan. "It's obvious. Why lock a boathouse unless something important is inside?"

Tristan read the story twice more while they argued. He was learning to perceive hints that weren't stated outright, the way you could feel rain coming before a cloud appeared. But something about the boathouse bothered him. The story spent three whole sentences on it, bright and shiny, like a sign with flashing arrows. The umbrella got one quiet sentence. He tested a simple idea: he underlined every hint, then crossed out the ones the author seemed too eager for him to notice. The umbrella survived. The boathouse didn't.

"Chase," Tristan said, "why would the author hand you the answer on page one?"

"Because authors reward smart readers."

"Or because it's a trick." Tristan flipped to the glossary in his book club handbook and found the term. "It's called a red herring. A false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion, so not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing."

Chase stared at his cookie as if it had betrayed him. "So the boathouse is bait."

"Robust bait," Tristan said. "It even has a lock on it."

They read the ending aloud together. The flood came, just as the umbrella promised, and the boathouse turned out to hold nothing but rusty oars. The thief had been the mail carrier all along, a character mentioned once, quietly, wearing rain boots.

Mr. Holloway wandered over with his coffee. "Verdict?"

"Red herring," the three of them said at once.

He laughed. "That phenomenon gets you all the first time. It got me in eighth grade. I blamed the author for a week."

Chase broke his cookie in half and handed a piece to Tristan. "For the umbrella. Next time I'm trusting the quiet clues."

"Next time," Tristan said, "we're reading the ending twice."

Elisha raised the cardboard detective dog's paw in a toast, and they all tapped it.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish nouns have grammatical gender, so a male dog is "el perro" and a female dog is "la perra."
story:
Taylor slid her Spanish worksheet across the library table and tapped the empty line at the bottom. The assignment said to write five full sentences about her family and pets, and so far she had four. The fifth was supposed to be about her dog, Rex, but Rex had died in the spring, and she had not figured out how to write about him yet, or whether she even wanted to.

"Tengo una hermana," Trinity read over her shoulder, chewing the end of her pencil. "Okay, that's 'I have a sister.' You forgot the accent, but Ms. Bighorn will know what you mean."

Jase was slouched two chairs away, writing fast, the way he did when he wanted to finish first. His dog, Pepper, was famous in their grade for having once eaten an entire birthday cake off a picnic table, so Taylor was not surprised that his first sentence was about her. "Tengo el perro," he announced. "Pepper is the best dog in the world. Tengo el perro."

Something snagged in Taylor's mind, the way a sleeve catches on a nail. She stared at his sentence. Last week they had learned "el gato" for the cat in the textbook photo, and "la gallina" for the hen in the story Ms. Bighorn had read aloud. El for one animal, la for another. She pulled the textbook toward her and flipped pages, watching for the pattern the way you monitor a fish tank for one specific fish, not staring, just waiting for it to swim past. Gato, el. Perra, la. Perro, el.

"Jase," she said slowly, "Pepper's a girl, right?"

"Duh. She had puppies last year."

Taylor turned the book so he could see the two vocabulary entries side by side. "Look. A male dog is el perro, and a female dog is la perra. Different word, different el and la." The library smelled like old carpet and the lemon cleaner the janitor used on the tables, and somewhere behind the shelves a printer clattered out pages. Jase leaned in, frowning at the print as if it might change while he watched.

"So I just called my girl dog a boy dog," he said. "In front of everybody."

"In a sentence, yeah." Taylor tested her idea before she said it out loud, because Ms. Bighorn was always telling them to check their work. If perro was male and perra was female, then Trinity's cat sentence should work the same way. "Trinity, is Sushi a boy or a girl?"

"Girl," said Trinity. "Tengo la gata."

That settled it. Taylor felt the click of the rule fitting together, small and satisfying. It had seemed like random els and las scattered everywhere, but they were not random at all; the words themselves carried the difference, and you had to know your animal before you could pick the right one.

Jase scratched out his sentence and wrote "Tengo la perra Pepper" in his cramped handwriting, then looked at it and looked at Taylor. "I thought Spanish was just, like, swapping English words out one at a time," he admitted. "It's more like a code with its own rules. That's actually kind of cool." He said it grudgingly, the way he admitted anything.

Taylor turned back to her own paper. She thought about Rex, brown and scruffy, asleep on the kitchen floor with his paws twitching. Then she picked up her pencil and wrote, "Tenía el perro Rex." I had a male dog named Rex. It was a small sentence for such a big absence, but it was true in both languages, and somehow that helped. She read it once more, quietly, under the hum of the library lights.

"Tengo la perra Pepper," Jase said to nobody in particular, "y ella es la mejor del mundo."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
Mia's squad had been sitting in the castle lobby for ten minutes because Sasha refused to start the match until she finished her story. "So I found this old blog," Sasha was saying, headset crackling, "from when we were like, eight. Mine. It's still up."

"That's impossible," Mia said. She was parachuting her character off the castle wall over and over, just to have something to do. "You deleted that thing in fourth grade. You told me you deleted it."

"Deleted from the internet," said Thatcher, who had joined mid-conversation as usual. "It's called the Wayback Machine. Since 1996, the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and anyone can look at old versions of websites. My brother showed me." A pause. "There's a photo of you in a clown wig, by the way, Sasha. Holding your street sign."

The lobby went quiet except for the match-making music. "My street sign," Sasha said slowly. "With the number on it."

Mia landed her character on a turret and stopped moving. She could infer the rest without asking: the blog post had a picture, the picture had a location, and somewhere out there the whole package was sitting in an archive where literally anyone could browse it. She'd posted things when she was eight too. Her old handle was something embarrassing involving the word "cupcake," and she could not for the life of her remember how much of her actual life she'd put on it.

"I'm checking mine," she announced. She tabbed out, typed the name of the old blog host, then her old handle. Nothing. She sat back, then leaned in again. Maybe the site needed the exact address. She dug through her memory, tried a different spelling, and there it was: a snapshot from 2019, gray and old-looking, with her banner still on it. CupcakeSparkles. Her avatar. And a post titled "My House Tour!!" with nine photos, including a very clear shot of her front door, her house number, and the name of her street on the mailbox.

"Found it," she said. "Guess who posted her entire address when she was eight."

"No way," said Thatcher.

"Way." She screenshotted it, then read his next message out loud. "He says, and I quote, 'delete it.'"

"You can't delete it," Sasha said. "It's an archive. That's the whole point. That's why I'm telling you this instead of crying about the clown wig."

Mia looked at the photo of her mailbox. Her brother's old blog currency had been silly drawings, but apparently hers had been home tours. "Okay," she said. "New rule. From now on we post pictures of our characters, not our houses." She tabbed back into the game and hit ready. "Now can we please start the match before I find anything else?"

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: Mawsynram, in India's Meghalaya state, is often called the wettest place on Earth, averaging nearly 12 meters of rain a year.
story:
Juliette stood in front of Ms. Sun's classroom after the last bell, holding a shoebox she had turned into a tiny rice paddy. "I still don't get how to explain a monsoon," she said. "I have to present tomorrow, and every time I try, it comes out like a dictionary threw up."

Ms. Sun smiled the way she did when she was about to make you figure something out yourself. "Then stop trying to explain it. Show it. What have you got in that box?"

"Rice, dirt, and a very confused paper sun taped to a popsicle stick." Juliette set the box on the counter by the window, where the afternoon light hit it. "Elliana says the monsoon is just rain. Darcy says it's wind. They can't both be right."

"Can't they?" Ms. Sun said, and walked away, which was so typical.

Juliette glared at the box. Then she filled a tray with water and slid it next to her shoebox paddy, because rice fields in South Asia are basically giant puddles, and she wanted to see what happened when the sun beat down on both. She taped a plastic bag over the top to trap the air. It looked ridiculous, like a greenhouse built by raccoons, but she wrote MONSOON MODEL on it anyway. She watched the bag. Nothing. She moved the whole thing under the heat lamp from the reptile cage nobody used since the science room lizard, poor Steve, went extinct, or at least stopped coming to school. The bag slowly fogged. Droplets formed, grew heavy, and fell back onto the dirt in fat, irregular splats.

"Wait," Juliette whispered. The rain didn't fall evenly. It came in bursts, then paused, then burst again. The dampness in the bag seemed to fluctuate, swelling and shrinking like the whole thing was breathing. So the rain wasn't just rain, and the wind wasn't just wind; the monsoon was a whole pattern, wet season and dry season trading places, and rice farmers timed their planting to it because a field that's flooded on purpose needs a sky that floods it for free.

The next day, Elliana and Darcy sat in the front row, ready to argue. Juliette set down her shoebox, the fogged bag, and a postcard she'd found at her mom's travel agency showing a rain-lashed green hillside. "Before I start," she said, "quiz question. The wettest place on Earth is called Mawsynram, in India's Meghalaya state, and it gets nearly twelve meters of rain a year. That's twelve of me, stacked."

Darcy's mouth fell open. "Twelve meters? It would drown Steve twice."

"Steve is a lizard, he'd love it," Elliana said. "Also, are you okay? You're grinning like you invented weather."

"I sort of did." Juliette flicked on the heat lamp. "Watch the bag. This is a rice field, this is the sun, and this, my friends, is a monsoon in a shoebox." The first droplet swelled on the plastic, trembled, and let go.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: French possessive words agree with the thing owned, not the owner, so "sa mère" can mean either "his mother" or "her mother."
story:
Piper slid her French worksheet across the library table until it sat exactly between her and Aylan. The task was to write five sentences about her family and her pets, full sentences, no single words allowed, and Mr. Nasser had said he would listen to each of them read aloud on Friday. Rain streaked the tall windows, and the overhead light caught the translucent page protector on the dictionary so that it gleamed like a sheet of ice. Piper had written four sentences already. The fifth one was the problem.

"Sa mère adore le café," she read off her rough draft. "That's for the part about my mom loving coffee."

Aylan frowned at his own paper. "Wait. Whose mom?"

"Mine. Obviously."

"It doesn't say that." He tapped the words with his pencil. "Sa mère. I wrote the same thing for my mom. Look." He turned his paper around, and there it was, letter for letter, sa mère, on both pages, even though Piper's mother was her mother and Aylan's mother was his.

Piper sat back. She checked the dictionary anyway, running her finger down the entry, and the examples did not help. She tried changing the word to son mère, because son felt like it should match a son or a daughter, the person doing the owning. That looked wrong the moment she wrote it. So she flipped through her notebook to the page where Mr. Nasser had written model sentences about families. In every single one, the possessive word matched the thing that came after it, not the person before it. Sa chatte. Son chien. Sa mère. The pattern held down the whole page, and it finally clicked: the words cared about the mother, the cat, the dog, and not at all about Piper or Aylan.

"So when I say sa mère," Piper said slowly, "you can't tell if I mean my mom or your mom."

"Or anybody's mom," Aylan said. He grinned, then stopped grinning. "That's a problem. Mr. Nasser will think I described your family by mistake. I want him to know I actually did the work. He keeps saying my sentences are too short, and this time I wrote real ones." He pulled his paper closer like he might submerge the whole thing under his arm and start over.

"No, don't rewrite it," Piper said. "We test it. I'll say my sentence to you, and you ask me whose mom. If the question works, we're fine." She straightened up in her chair, cleared her throat, and read aloud, "Sa mère adore le café."

"Whose mother?" Aylan asked immediately.

"Mine," Piper said. "See? It works. Tomorrow we tell Mr. Nasser we need to ask each other questions after every sentence, because that's the only way anyone finds out."

Aylan copied the question onto his paper, Whose mother?, right under his sentence, and underlined it twice.

"That's my diagnosis," he said. "French is a mystery novel, and every sentence is missing the last page."

Piper laughed quietly, so the librarian at the desk wouldn't look up, and wrote the question under her own sentence too. Then she added a sixth line about her dog: Son chien déteste la pluie.

"Whose dog?" Aylan asked.

Piper leaned forward and whispered, "You'll have to ask the dog."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: The number of protons decides which element an atom is: any atom with eight protons is oxygen, and an atom with seven protons is nitrogen.
story:
The science museum's chemistry hall had a wall-sized periodic table, and Edouard's class had twenty minutes before the bus left. Mr. Abdi handed out a quiz sheet with one question left blank on purpose: "If an oxygen atom somehow lost a proton, what would you have then?"

"Trick question," Jaylen said. "It would just be broken oxygen."

Edouard wasn't so sure. He stood in front of the wall and traced his finger along the boxes until he found oxygen. In the top corner of the box sat the number eight. Next to oxygen was nitrogen, with a seven. He had skimmed the little label under the table that morning, but he hadn't really read it, and now he leaned in again. Above the boxes it said: atomic number. He stared at that word, then at the eight, then at the seven.

"Okay," he said slowly, "so oxygen is number eight and nitrogen is number seven."

Priya came over from the hydrogen display, where she had been trying to make her reflection contract into the curved mirror beside it. "So what?"

"So the numbers are the protons." He tapped the wall. "That's the whole point of the number. And if oxygen somehow lost one proton, it wouldn't be broken oxygen. It would have seven protons." He dragged his finger one box to the left. "It would be nitrogen."

Jaylen shook his head. "That can't be right. Oxygen is oxygen because of what it does, right? It's the stuff you breathe."

"Any atom with eight protons is oxygen," Edouard said, reading the panel under the display case, which repeated it in plain print. "An atom with seven protons is nitrogen. That's what makes it that element. The proton count decides."

Jaylen looked at the wall for a long moment. His shoulders dropped. "So the quiz answer is nitrogen. Losing one proton turns it into a totally different thing." He rubbed his eyes. "I was sure it was a trick question. I changed my mind, and I hate that."

Mr. Abdi walked by collecting the sheets. "Answers, gentlemen, ladies. Bus in five."

Jaylen wrote his answer, then held the pencil up. "From your perspective this is fun. From mine it's disturbing. You're telling me the air is one proton away from being wrong."

"You'll live," Priya said. "You've had a chronic case of being wrong since September, and you keep surviving it."

On the bus, Edouard watched the museum shrink in the window and thought about how something nobody could ever see, one proton, was the only thing standing between two boxes on a wall. He pulled out his notebook, wrote 8 at the top of a page and 7 below it, and drew an arrow between them.

"One," he said, and underlined it twice.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Pianissimo, written pp, means very soft, and fortissimo, written ff, means very loud.
story:
The drum kit took up half of Shania's garage, and the old upright piano, inherited from a grandfather nobody remembered, took up most of the rest. Scarlett sat at its bench with the sheet music for "Moonlight Over Water" propped against the music stand, her fingers hovering above the keys. Shania twirled a drumstick and waited.

"From the top," Scarlett said. "And watch me this time, because we keep rushing the middle."

They had practiced the piece for two weeks, and it still fell apart in the same place every single time. The opening sounded fine, dreamy and rolling, but by the ending the whole thing turned into a wall of noise. Shania hit the cymbals like she was trying to provoke the neighbors into calling about it, and Scarlett pounded along to keep up, and the last eight measures dissolved into mush.

Shania's mom had even knocked on the garage door once, holding her ears, which Shania had treated as a compliment. That was the problem, Scarlett thought. Shania wanted the performance to end big and loud, a finish that would make the audience sit up. She wanted the drums to be the rudder of the whole piece, steering where it went. Scarlett just wanted it to sound right.

She looked at the last page again. Under the final measures sat two tiny letters, and above them, near the loud part in the middle, two different ones. She had assumed they were smudges or some kind of printing mistake. But now she noticed the same letters turning up in every piece in the folder. She fetched her music dictionary from her backpack, the one she'd bought at the used book sale and never opened, and looked up the first one.

"Shania," she said slowly, "come look at this."

Shania leaned over the piano, drumstick dangling from her fingers. "What?"

"Pianissimo, written pp, means very soft." Scarlett tapped the page. "That's what's marked on the ending. Very soft. Not louder. And ff means very loud. That's the middle part. We've been playing the whole thing exactly backward." She felt strangely buoyant, the way she did when a puzzle suddenly snapped together. All this time there had been a pattern hiding on the page, and they had stomped right past it.

"So the ending is supposed to shrink?" Shania looked wounded. "That's the opposite of a grand finish."

"Try it once," Scarlett said. "Just once. If it's terrible, you can hit everything as hard as you want."

Shania sighed like the weight of the world had landed on her shoulders, picked up her brushes instead of sticks, and counted them in with a whisper. Scarlett let her right hand drift down to almost nothing, and the last notes of "Moonlight Over Water" faded out like a tide going still.

"Okay," Shania admitted, brushing a cymbal so lightly it barely breathed. "That's kind of amazing. Do it again."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: On eye prescriptions, OD means the right eye and OS means the left eye, from the Latin oculus dexter and oculus sinister.
story:
Luca sat on the crinkly paper of the nurse's cot, holding his new prescription slip like it might bite him. The words OD and OS were typed beside two numbers, and beside those, in Mr. Bekele's careful handwriting, was a note that the glasses would arrive Thursday. Luca had read the slip eleven times since the eye doctor's office on Saturday, and every time the letters looked worse.

"OD," Lucien whispered from the doorway, because Lucien had promised to walk to the nurse's office with him and then refused to leave. "You know what that stands for? Ocular Disease." Luca's stomach dropped. "OS has to be Ocular Something worse," Lucien went on. "Why else would they hide it in Latin?"

That was exactly the part that bugged Luca. Nobody hides good news in Latin. But Mr. Bekele was already coming back with the folder, so Luca did the only reasonable thing, which was to shove the slip under his math workbook and pretend to examine the poster about lichen on the wall, which had nothing to do with anything but gave him somewhere to point his eyes. The poster said lichen was actually two organisms living together, a fungus and an alga, and Luca's brain snagged on that even in the middle of his panic. Two things, one word. Two letters, one slip.

He thought about Latin class. Oculus meant eye; he was almost sure. He'd seen dexter before too, in a word for right-handed. And sinister meant left, which was unfair to left-handed people but that was Latin for you. He tried it out against the paper, covering one letter at a time. If OD meant the right eye, then the number beside it belonged to his right eye, and the doctor had said his right eye was the blurrier one at the board. Luca covered his left eye and squinted at the eye chart hanging on the wall. Blurrier. Right. The letters weren't a disease at all; they were an address label.

"Mr. Bekele," Luca said, holding up the slip before he could lose his nerve, "on here, does OD mean my right eye and OS my left eye? Like, oculus dexter and oculus sinister?"

Mr. Bekele smiled and tapped the two letters. "OD is the right eye, OS is the left. Straight from the Latin."

Lucien's mouth fell open. "So it's not a disease?"

"It's an address," Luca said, and it felt inevitable, the way the whole terrifying code had cracked open the second he stopped guessing and started testing. The two boys compromised on what to do next: Lucien wanted to go look up more Latin, and Luca wanted to walk to the window to see whether the tree across the yard had leaves he could actually count. They did both, fast, and Luca counted eleven leaves on one branch before the bell even rang.
